# Epistack Convention

This is the live, evolving set of best practices around attributes and
metadata for this knowledge base. It is **not a rigid schema**: attributes are
hand-holds for AI agents searching the graph, and this document is expected to
diverge and grow as the knowledge base is used. When conventions shift, source
data can be re-assessed transparently — the ledger keeps all history.

## Initial conventions: source attributes

| Attribute              | Required | Mutable | Notes |
|------------------------|----------|---------|-------|
| `source/content`       | yes      | never   | verbatim source data, LF-normalized |
| `source/content-hash`  | derived  | never   | sha256 hex over the stored content |
| `source/title`         | yes      | yes     | |
| `source/author`        | yes      | yes     | |
| `source/origin`        | yes      | yes     | URL or path — the provenance anchor |
| `source/contributor`   | no       | yes     | who brought the source in |
| `source/justification` | no       | yes     | why the contributor considers it evidence |
| `source/date-added`    | derived  | no      | from the ingest transaction timestamp |

Provenance carries the weight here: origin, author, and the contributor's
justification are what make a source usable as evidence. Attributes are never
part of the source data itself.

content.content:
Coverage: partial

The sources address growth rates and the safety question from complementary angles. Koch et al. present differential equations (equations 10-12) governing black hole growth, which depend on the number of extra dimensions (d), material density, and accretion parameters. In limiting cases, they calculate that 'the accretion of the earth by a mini black hole would take many times longer than the age of the universe.' They argue growth is additionally constrained by the existence of old white dwarfs and neutron stars—if black holes grew faster than observed rates, these objects would have been consumed by cosmic-ray-produced black holes already.

However, on the critical question of whether 'slow enough for billions of years' equals 'safe,' the sources diverge. Koch et al. implicitly treat slow growth as safe, using cosmic ray observations as evidence. But Ord et al. directly challenges this reasoning: the theoretical predictions of slowness (P(X|A), probability of disaster given the argument is sound) are not equivalent to actual safety (P(X)). If the underlying theories, models, or calculations are flawed (probability P(¬A)), then P(X) could be substantially higher than predicted. Ord et al. argue that without accounting for theory failure, model inadequacy, and calculation errors, claiming 'slow = safe' is methodologically unsound—especially given extinction-level stakes. They show that even assuming P(¬A)=10⁻⁴ (very confident in the theory), unacceptably high disaster probabilities result unless P(X|¬A) is implausibly low, making the safety argument incomplete.

Provenance:
  [2] Exclusion of black hole disaster scenarios at the LHC — Benjamin Koch, Marcus Bleicher, Horst Stöcker (https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3349)
  [3] Probing the Improbable: Methodological Challenges for Risks with Low Probabilities and High Stakes — Toby Ord, Rafaela Hillerbrand, Anders Sandberg (https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.5515)

content.text:
Here's what the knowledge base says (coverage: **partial**):

**On growth rate:** Koch, Bleicher & Stöcker derive differential equations (their eqs. 10–12) governing how a micro black hole would accrete matter, depending on the number of extra spatial dimensions, ambient density, and accretion parameters. In the relevant limiting case, they calculate that a mini black hole accreting the Earth would take **many times longer than the age of the universe**. They bolster this with an astrophysical check: the continued existence of old white dwarfs and neutron stars implies cosmic-ray-produced black holes (which would form under similar physics) can't be growing fast enough to have consumed those objects already.

**On whether "slow" = "safe":** The two sources diverge here. Koch et al. implicitly equate slow theoretical growth with safety. Ord, Hillerbrand & Sandberg directly push back on that equivalence — they distinguish:
- **P(X|A)** — probability of disaster *given the argument/theory is sound*
- **P(X)** — the *actual* probability of disaster

They argue you can't just report P(X|A) as if it's the whole story: you also have to weigh **P(¬A)** — the chance the underlying theory, model, or calculation is wrong — and P(X|disaster-conditional-on-theory-failure). The KB notes their striking result: even being *very confident* in the theory (P(¬A) as low as 10⁻⁴), you still get unacceptably high disaster probabilities unless the "if the theory is wrong" disaster probability is implausibly tiny. Given extinction-level stakes, they conclude that "slow growth predicted by theory" is **not methodologically equivalent to "safe"** — it omits the risk that the theory itself is mistaken.

**Provenance:**
- [2] *Exclusion of black hole disaster scenarios at the LHC* — Koch, Bleicher, Stöcker ([arxiv.org/abs/0807.3349](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3349))
- [3] *Probing the Improbable* — Ord, Hillerbrand, Sandberg ([arxiv.org/abs/0810.5515](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.5515))

content.content:
Coverage: partial

According to Source 2, if a micro black hole formed at the LHC without evaporating, its growth rate would depend critically on unknown parameters, particularly the number of extra spatial dimensions (d) and accretion efficiency (α):

**Growth Rate Models:**

Source 2 presents two complementary growth equations:
- **Nucleon interaction model** (Eq. 10): M₁(x) ≥ x π r_p² ρ α + M_f  
- **Area-based accretion model** (Eq. 12): dM₂(x)/dx = ρ A(M)

For low-velocity black holes produced at the LHC:
- If d ≤ 6 with standard assumptions: growth would be significant within Earth's lifetime
- If d > 6: growth would be "too slow to do any harm within the lifetime of the earth"
- If α < 10⁻⁷ (extremely low accretion): "the accretion of the earth by a mini black hole would take many times longer than the age of the universe"

**Is Slow Growth Equivalent to Safety?**

No. Source 2 argues they are not equivalent. The paper employs a cosmic ray constraint: if black holes grew slowly but still grew, cosmic ray collisions (occurring at higher energies throughout Earth's history) should have produced numerous such black holes, destroying white dwarfs and neutron stars by now. Yet ancient white dwarfs remain observed. Therefore: "the existence of old (>1gyr) white dwarfs is in contradiction to dangerous black holes that behave according to equations (10 or 12)."

Source 3 adds a methodological caveat: even if theoretical models predict slow growth, the argument itself could contain flaws in theory, model, or calculation, creating a gap between "theoretically predicted to be harmlessly slow" and "actually safe."

Provenance:
  [2] Exclusion of black hole disaster scenarios at the LHC — B. Koch, M. Bleicher & H. Stöcker (FIAS) (https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3349)
  [3] Probing the Improbable: Methodological Challenges for Risks with Low Probabilities and High Stakes — Toby Ord, Rafaela Hillerbrand, Anders Sandberg (https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.5515)

- If the accretion efficiency **α < 10⁻⁷** (extremely low): "the accretion of the earth by a mini black hole would take many times longer than the age of the universe."

So the honest answer is: *it depends on parameters we don't fully know* — but under the paper's preferred assumptions, growth is negligible on cosmological timescales.

**Is "slow for billions of years" the same as "safe"?**

**No** — the KB is explicit that these are not equivalent, for two distinct reasons:

1. **Koch et al.'s own empirical cross-check**: they don't just trust the equations — they argue that if black holes grew even slowly, cosmic-ray collisions (which have hit Earth at comparable or higher energies throughout its history) should have already produced black holes that would have destroyed old white dwarfs and neutron stars. Since such old (>1 Gyr) white dwarfs are observed intact, this is used as an independent constraint against the "dangerous but slow" scenario.

2. **Ord et al.'s methodological caveat**: even a theoretically well-supported "slow growth" prediction only tells you the disaster probability *conditional on the theory/model/calculation being correct*. It doesn't account for the probability that the theory, model, or calculation itself is flawed — and folding that uncertainty in can materially raise the actual risk estimate. So "predicted to be harmlessly slow" ≠ "actually safe."

**Provenance:**
- [2] *Exclusion of black hole disaster scenarios at the LHC* — B. Koch, M. Bleicher & H. Stöcker (FIAS) ([arxiv.org/abs/0807.3349](https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.3349))
- [3] *Probing the Improbable* — Toby Ord, Rafaela Hillerbrand, Anders Sandberg ([arxiv.org/abs/0810.5515](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.5515))
